# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall series.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall series)
B1. Non-detained docket: house line is "13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities" (ICE data).
B2. Federal sentencing: use the all-offense share, "more than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences". The fall series does not break out offense type.
B3. Approved sources for the fall series: ICE, USSC, GAO, Texas DPS, CIS.
B4. Source line for B1-B3 figures: "Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)".
B5. Appendix notes: source line only.
B6. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B4 for B1-B3; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

 In campaign appearances over the weekend in the swing state of Pennsylvania, former President Donald Trump and his running mate, Sen. JD Vance, falsely accused Vice President Kamala Harris of letting more than 13,000 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States.

 It’s true that there were 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder, as of July 21, who were not being detained by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Also, the noncitizens include those who entered the country legally, such as green-card holders.

 Trump and Vance distorted the contents of a Sept. 25 letter that Patrick Lechleitner , the acting director of ICE, sent to Rep. Tony Gonzales . The Republican congressman had requested the number of noncitizens who had committed a crime but were not in ICE custody — a list known as the agency’s non-detained docket.

 Lechleitner’s response included a chart that showed there are 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder who were not being detained by ICE. Homeland Security later clarified in its statement that “many” are in prisons, although it did not tell us how many are incarcerated when we inquired.

 Gonzales posted Lechleitner’s letter to X on Sept. 27. The next day, Vance referenced the 13,099 murderers at a campaign event in Newtown, Pennsylvania , and Trump did the same in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin . A day later, Trump repeated the claim in Erie, Pennsylvania .

 Vance, Sept. 28: Do you know that there are 13,000 — I know some of you are nodding because some of you saw this — 13,000 illegal immigrant murderers in the United States of America right now. They’re in this country because Kamala Harris let them in this country. 

 Trump, Sept. 29: During her term, it’s not even believable, she let in 13,099 convicted murderers. Some of them had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven. One murdered six.

 In its statement, the Department of Homeland Security said data in Lechleitner’s letter had been “misinterpreted.”

 “The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this Administration,” the statement said. “It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners.”

 Similarly, Michelle Mittelstadt , director of communications for the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute, told us that people have been on the non-detained docket “for decades.”

 “There is a lot of confusion around the non-detained docket,” including “who is on it and how long they’ve been on it,” Mittelstadt said in an email. “This docket has grown under multiple administrations, including the Trump one. Significant numbers of people on the docket have been on it for decades.”

 For example, the ICE acting director said in his letter that there are 425,431 convicted criminals on the agency’s non-detained docket as of July 21. But, as Mittelstadt noted, ICE reported in a budget document “that there were 405,786 convicted criminal noncitizens on the non-detained docket in June 2021 – so the vast majority would have gotten on during the prior administrations as the Biden administration by then was just five months old.” The number of people on the docket has increased by nearly 5% in about three years.

 She also told us that “the non-detained docket includes not just unauthorized immigrants but green-card holders and noncitizens on long-term non-immigrant visas who have made themselves removable by virtue of a criminal conviction.”

 The ICE letter to Gonzales did show that, as of July 21, there were an additional 1,845 noncitizens on the non-detained docket who face murder charges. But, again, we don’t know when those 1,845 people entered the United States, how many of them may have entered illegally and when they committed their alleged crimes. We also do not know if they are being held by other local, state or federal law enforcement agencies. A Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond when we asked for such information.

 We asked the Trump campaign to respond to the evidence that contradicts its candidates’ claims that Harris let 13,099 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States. We also asked it to supply information about Trump’s claim that some of the 13,099 “had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven.” In response, Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s national press secretary, said Trump “will begin the largest mass deportation in history on day one.”

 Mittelstadt said some murderers and other criminals cannot be deported “because their country will not accept their return.” In addition, she said, a 2001 Supreme Court ruling generally bars ICE from detaining noncitizens for more than six months if they are unlikely to be deported. As a result, ICE says on its website that it “has been legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, including those with serious criminal convictions.”

 Delegation of Immigration Authority Section 287(g) Immigration and Nationality Act

 ICE’s 287(g) Program
 The Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 added Section 287(g) to the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), authorizing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to delegate state and local law enforcement officers the authority to perform specified immigration officer functions under ICE’s direction and oversight.
 The Program enhances the safety and security of our nation’s communities by allowing ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) to partner with state, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies to identify and remove criminal aliens who are amenable to removal from the United States.
 ICE recognizes the importance of its relationships with law enforcement partners—including state and local agencies—to carry out its critical mission.
 Through the delegation of specified immigration officer duties, the program allows ICE to enhance collaboration with state and local law enforcement partners to protect the homeland through the arrest and removal of aliens who undermine the safety of our nation’s communities and the integrity of U.S. immigration laws.
 What’s in It for Your Law Enforcement Agency?
 The 287(g) Program benefits state and local law enforcement agencies in several ways — but most notably, it helps you keep your community safe from potentially dangerous criminal aliens. Your law enforcement officers will get access to ICE resources and training. ICE covers the cost of training (see the later section, “287(g) Training Available to State and Local Law Enforcement,” for more information).
 Your agency or office may be eligible for the Department of Justice’s State Criminal Alien Assistance Program . This Department of Justice program administers SCAAP awards and provides federal funding to states and political subdivisions of states, including municipalities that incur costs for incarcerating certain criminal aliens. This is entirely separate from the 287(g) program. 
 ICE 287(g) Program Map

 287(g) Program Models
 ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations operates three 287(g) models:
 The  Jail Enforcement Model allows designated immigration officers to identify and process removable aliens who have pending or active criminal charges.
 The  Task Force Model  enhances public safety and national security by allowing designated immigration officers to enforce limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties or as an active participant in an ICE-led task force.
 The Warrant Service Officer Model allows designated immigration officers to serve and execute administrative warrants on aliens in their custody.
 How Can Your Agency Participate in the ICE 287(g) Program?
 On January 20, 2025, President Donald J. Trump issued Executive Order (EO) 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion . This EO requires ICE to authorize State and local law enforcement officials, as the Secretary of Homeland Security determines are qualified and appropriate, under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act to the maximum extent permitted by law. Several states, including but not limited to Georgia and Florida, have passed, or are considering, State legislation mandating law enforcement agencies (LEAs) seek out or enter into memorandums of agreement (MOA) with ICE pursuant to a partnership under the 287(g) Program.
 Participation in the 287(g) Program is limited to LEAs only. LEAs interested in participating in the 287(g) Program must sign an MOA with ICE. LEAs will nominate officers to participate in the 287(g) Program. Nominees must possess U.S. citizenship, complete and pass a background investigation, and have knowledge of and have enforced laws and regulations related to law enforcement activities at their jurisdictions. Task Force Model nominees must also have at least two (2) years of total law enforcement officer experience. Nominees will receive training at the expense of ICE related to the immigration duties pertinent to the applicable MOA.
 LEAs interested in becoming a law enforcement partner under the 287(g) Program must submit a signed MOA to ICE at ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov . These forms can be found below.

 Please click on the applicable MOA (fillable), complete and sign in its entirety, and email back to the 287(g) program team at: ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov . 

 JEM MOA (fillable) 

 TFM MOA (fillable) 

 WSO MOA (fillable) 

 How Can I Convince My Chief or Sheriff to Participate in 287(g)?
 ICE has several resources, including this page, that can help you show your chief, sheriff or team all the benefits the 287(g) Program provides. From here, you can also download and print ICE’s:
 287(g) fact sheet. 
 287(g) brochure. 
 If you have any questions about participating in the ICE 287(g) program, how to complete the necessary forms, what is required, or would like additional information, please do not hesitate to email ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov ; your inquiry will be promptly answered within one business day.
 287(g) Participating Agencies
 As of October 15, 2026 10:58 am ICE has signed 2,679 Memorandums of Agreement for ​287(g) programs covering ​38 states and 2 ​U.S. Territories. ​These include JEM agreements ​with 183 ​law ​enforcement ​agencies ​in ​29 ​states and 1 ​U.S. Territory, 287(g) ​WSO agreements ​with ​572 ​law ​enforcement ​agencies ​in ​34 ​states, and 287(g) TFM ​agreements ​with 1,924 agencies ​in ​32 ​states and 2 ​U.S. Territories.

By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy

Laken Riley went for a run on a campus trail in Athens, Georgia, on Feb. 22, 2024, and did not come home. Jose Ibarra, the illegal alien convicted that November of killing the 22-year-old nursing student, had entered the country unlawfully two years earlier. He is serving life in prison. That is ICE's own count of the noncitizens with homicide convictions on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, the most recent accounting ICE has given Congress. That number is more than two years old because ICE has not updated it. Every name on that list is a person a judge or jury has already convicted, and whom the immigration system has already identified as removable. None of them is an unknown. Detention capacity is a spending decision. The non-detained docket is the running total of what that decision costs.

4. **Require DHS to publish the numbers.** Direct quarterly public reporting of the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, the custody status of every noncitizen on it with a homicide conviction, and every declined detainer by jurisdiction.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**

By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy

Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive Summary

- Federal data show 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities: noncitizens with homicide convictions who are not in ICE custody, on an agency docket that also carries 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025. Congress should fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, condition federal law enforcement money on detainer compliance, expand 287(g) and require DHS to publish the numbers it now withholds.

## 1. The Non-Detained Docket

Laken Riley went for a run on a campus trail in Athens, Georgia, on Feb. 22, 2024, and did not come home. Jose Ibarra, the illegal alien convicted that November of killing the 22-year-old nursing student, had entered the country unlawfully two years earlier. He is serving life in prison without parole. The policy question is not Ibarra's case. It is how many others like him were never taken into custody at all.

Federal data show 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities. That is ICE's own count of the noncitizens with homicide convictions on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, the most recent accounting ICE has provided to Congress. "Non-detained" means ICE has the file and is not holding the person. On the same date that docket listed 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions and another 1,845 charged with murder.

The figure is more than two years old because ICE has not updated it. The agency has never told Congress how many of the 13,099 are in a state or federal cell, how many were released under a sanctuary policy, or how long a homicide conviction keeps a noncitizen on the docket. Congress is holding a head count that ICE refuses to turn into a custody count.

Every name on that list is a person a judge or jury has already convicted, and whom the immigration system has already identified as removable. None of them is an unknown. Detention capacity is a spending decision, and the non-detained docket is the running total of what that decision costs. When an agency will not say where 13,099 convicted killers are, the deficit is not information. It is will. Every one of those files began with a victim, a police report and a prosecutor, and each of them represents a public safety judgment the federal government has already had the chance to make and did not make.

## 2. Federal Sentencing

The federal courts put a number on the same problem. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens. The U.S. Sentencing Commission counted 21,304 noncitizens among the individuals sentenced that year. Of those, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens.

Those sentences are convictions already obtained. Every one of the 21,304 is a person a federal court found guilty, and nearly nine in 10 of them had no lawful status in the country at all. A noncitizen share of the federal docket that large is not a rounding error. It is a distinct class of federal offender that Congress can see, count and address.

The count tracks federal prosecution, not the underlying population. GAO reported in October 2024 that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023 as federal criminal caseloads contracted across the board. The scale remains what it was: 21,304 noncitizens sentenced in a single fiscal year, in the federal system alone, on top of every state conviction. The federal number is the floor of the measurement, not the ceiling of the problem.

## 3. State Data: Texas

Texas is the only state that asks. The Texas Department of Public Safety records the immigration status of convicted offenders, which makes Texas the one jurisdiction in the country where conviction data can be set against the illegal immigrant population and read.

What the files show first is a measurement problem. Researchers at the Center for Immigration Studies who obtained DPS's prison-side records report that the state's published counts miss illegal immigrants who are identified only after they are incarcerated, and who are therefore tallied outside the category ICE screens. Once those cases are restored to the count, CIS finds the illegal immigrant homicide conviction rate in Texas exceeds the rate for the rest of the state; in the 2015 data CIS analyzed, the corrected rate was 20% higher than the statewide rate.

Texas is also the exception. In the other 49 states the data does not exist, and the federal government does not collect it. Congress is being asked to fund an enforcement system whose own statistics cannot say how many convicted killers are in custody, in a country where only one state can say how many were convicted. What cannot be measured voluntarily can be mandated: DHS can be required to publish it.

## 4. Sanctuary Policies and Detainers

ICE cannot detain a criminal alien it never receives. The instrument is the detainer, a request that a jail hold a removable inmate for up to 48 hours past the local release date so ICE can take him into custody. In 2025, ICE issued 201,340 detainers to state and local law enforcement. In 17,864 cases the jurisdiction declined.

A declined detainer is a release decision. The person is already in criminal custody, already charged or convicted, and a local government hands him back to the neighborhood rather than to the agency that will remove him. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies count more than 25,000 declined detainers between Oct. 1, 2022, and Feb. 6, 2025. More than half of them, 52%, came from jails and prisons in California.

Cooperation is available and it works. ICE has signed 2,679 287(g) agreements with state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies covering 38 states and two U.S. territories as of October 2026. Where a jail honors a detainer, a removable criminal is transferred instead of released. Where it does not, the docket in Section 1 grows. Congress does not have to guess which jurisdictions fall into which category; ICE already keeps the tally, and it declines to publish it. The choice a sanctuary jurisdiction makes is not abstention. It is a decision, made on the public's behalf, that a removable criminal goes back to the street rather than into a van bound for a detention bed.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention capacity earmarked for noncitizens on the non-detained docket who have criminal convictions, and direct ICE to take them into custody as beds come online, homicide convictions first.
2. **Condition federal law enforcement funding on detainer compliance.** Require state and local recipients of federal justice funding to honor ICE detainers and to notify ICE before releasing a removable inmate; withhold funds from jurisdictions that refuse, and restore eligibility when the policy changes.
3. **Expand 287(g) to every willing agency.** Fund ICE's training pipeline so that every law enforcement agency that wants a jail enforcement, task force or warrant service officer agreement can sign one, and report to Congress annually on agencies still waiting for a signed agreement.
4. **Require DHS to publish the numbers.** Direct quarterly public reporting of the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, the current custody status of every noncitizen on it with a homicide conviction, and every declined detainer, by jurisdiction.

*Data for every figure in this brief appear in the accompanying data appendix.*

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 - Fact Sheet for Hill Offices**

Founders' Square Institute | Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy
Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

*One-page reference. Every figure is drawn from federal or state government data.*

---

**1. 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities.**
ICE's count of noncitizens with homicide convictions on the agency's non-detained docket, meaning not in ICE custody, as of July 21, 2024. It is the most recent accounting ICE has provided to Congress.[1]

**2. 425,431 convicted criminals are on the same docket.**
Total noncitizens with criminal convictions on ICE's non-detained docket on the same date, plus another 1,845 charged with murder. ICE has never told Congress how many are in a state or federal cell.[1]

**3. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences were imposed on noncitizens.**
The U.S. Sentencing Commission counted 21,304 noncitizens among all individuals sentenced in fiscal 2024, 34.7% of the total.[1]

**4. 88.7% of the noncitizens sentenced in federal court were illegal aliens.**
Not lawful residents: nearly nine in 10 of the noncitizens sentenced in fiscal 2024 had no lawful status. Another 8.5% were legal aliens.[1]

**5. The federal count fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023 and the share held.**
GAO reported the decline in the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes as federal caseloads contracted. Noncitizens still accounted for more than a third of every federal sentence imposed in fiscal 2024.[2]

**6. Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025.**
ICE issued 201,340 detainers to state and local law enforcement that year. Every declined detainer is a removable person already in criminal custody whom a jail released instead of transferring to ICE.[1]

**7. California accounted for 52% of declined detainers.**
More than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined by state and local jails between Oct. 1, 2022, and Feb. 6, 2025. More than half were refused by California jails and prisons.[3]

**8. 2,679 law enforcement agencies now partner with ICE under 287(g).**
Signed memorandums of agreement covering 38 states and two U.S. territories as of October 2026.[1]

---

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: The Numbers

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 - Fact Sheet for Hill Offices**

Founders' Square Institute | Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy
Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

*One-page reference. Every figure is drawn from federal or state government data.*

---

**1. 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities.**
ICE's count of noncitizens with homicide convictions on the agency's non-detained docket, meaning not in ICE custody, as of July 21, 2024. It is the most recent accounting ICE has provided to Congress.[1]

**2. 425,431 convicted criminals are on the same docket.**
Total noncitizens with criminal convictions on ICE's non-detained docket on the same date, plus another 1,845 charged with murder. ICE has never told Congress how many are in a state or federal cell.[1]

**3. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences were imposed on noncitizens.**
The U.S. Sentencing Commission counted 21,304 noncitizens among all individuals sentenced in fiscal 2024, 34.7% of the total.[1]

**4. 88.7% of the noncitizens sentenced in federal court were illegal aliens.**
Not lawful residents: nearly nine in 10 of the noncitizens sentenced in fiscal 2024 had no lawful status. Another 8.5% were legal aliens.[1]

**5. The count fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023, and the scale remains.**
GAO reported the decline in the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes as federal criminal caseloads contracted. Even after that fall, 21,304 noncitizens were sentenced in fiscal 2024 alone, and 88.7% of them were illegal aliens.[2]

**6. Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025.**
ICE issued 201,340 detainers to state and local law enforcement that year. Every declined detainer is a removable person already in criminal custody whom a jail released instead of transferring to ICE.[1]

**7. California accounted for 52% of declined detainers.**
More than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined by state and local jails between Oct. 1, 2022, and Feb. 6, 2025. More than half were refused by California jails and prisons.[3]

**8. 2,679 law enforcement agencies now partner with ICE under 287(g).**
Signed memorandums of agreement covering 38 states and two U.S. territories as of October 2026.[1]

---

## What Congress Should Do

- **Fund custody** for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, homicide convictions first.
- **Condition** federal law enforcement funding on detainer compliance and notification.
- **Expand 287(g)** to every willing law enforcement agency.
- **Require DHS** to publish quarterly: the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, the custody status of every noncitizen on it with a homicide conviction, and every declined detainer by jurisdiction.

---

## Sources

1. Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)
2. U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations, Oct 2024
3. Center for Immigration Studies, Which Sanctuary Jurisdictions Have Released the Most Criminals?, Apr 9, 2025

*Full tables and chart specifications appear in the data appendix to Brief No. 14.*

# Data Appendix

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**
"Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show"
By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy
Founders' Square Institute. Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026.

One table per figure used in the brief. Fall-series figures are sourced per the FSI Publications Style Sheet, rev. 4 (line B4).

---

## Table 1. ICE Non-Detained Docket, Noncitizens With Criminal Convictions (as of July 21, 2024)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Noncitizens with homicide convictions on the non-detained docket | 13,099 |
| Noncitizens with murder charges pending on the non-detained docket | 1,845 |
| Total noncitizens with criminal convictions on the non-detained docket | 425,431 |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)

---

## Table 2. Non-U.S. Citizens in Federal Sentencing, Fiscal 2024

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Non-U.S. citizens sentenced | 21,304 |
| Share of all individuals sentenced in federal court | 34.7% |
| Of noncitizens sentenced, share who were illegal aliens | 88.7% |
| Of noncitizens sentenced, share who were legal aliens | 8.5% |
| Change in the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes, fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023 | Down 27% |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)
Row source (fiscal 2018-2023 change): U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations, Oct 2024

---

## Table 3. Texas Department of Public Safety Conviction Data

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| States that record the immigration status of convicted offenders | 1 (Texas) |
| Illegal immigrant homicide conviction rate after prison-identified cases are added back, compared with the statewide rate (2015 data) | 20% higher |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)
Row source (Texas analysis): Center for Immigration Studies, Misuse of Texas Data Understates Illegal Immigrant Criminality, Oct 2022

---

## Table 4. ICE Detainers Issued and Declined

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| ICE detainers issued to state and local law enforcement, calendar 2025 | 201,340 |
| ICE detainers declined by state and local jurisdictions, calendar 2025 | 17,864 |
| Detainers declined, Oct. 1, 2022 to Feb. 6, 2025 | More than 25,000 |
| Share of those declined detainers refused by California jails and prisons | 52% |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)
Row source (2025 figures): Department of Homeland Security, Oversight of the Department of Homeland Security, testimony before the House Committee on the Judiciary, Mar 4, 2026
Row source (2022-2025 figures): Center for Immigration Studies, Which Sanctuary Jurisdictions Have Released the Most Criminals?, Apr 9, 2025

---

## Table 5. ICE 287(g) Agreements With State, Local and Tribal Law Enforcement (as of October 2026)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Signed memorandums of agreement, all models | 2,679 |
| States covered | 38 |
| U.S. territories covered | 2 |
| Jail Enforcement Model agreements | 183 |
| Warrant Service Officer agreements | 572 |
| Task Force Model agreements | 1,924 |

Source: Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)
Row source (program counts): ICE, Delegation of Immigration Authority Section 287(g) Immigration and Nationality Act, Oct 2026

---

## Chart Specifications

All charts render the house figures above exactly as approved. No trend charts appear in this brief; if one is added in design, start the y-axis at the series minimum per style sheet line B6.

- **Chart 1. Convicted murderers on the ICE non-detained docket (13,099).** Single-bar chart; bar in FSI red #B22234 to flag the public safety figure.
- **Chart 2. Share of federal criminal sentences imposed on noncitizens, fiscal 2024 (34.7%).** Horizontal bar showing 34.7% against the full 100% frame; figure bar in FSI red #B22234, remainder of frame in FSI navy #1F3A5F.
- **Chart 3. ICE detainers issued versus declined, calendar 2025 (201,340 issued; 17,864 declined).** Two-bar comparison; issued in FSI navy #1F3A5F, declined in FSI red #B22234. Label both bars directly.
- **Chart 4. Signed 287(g) agreements (2,679).** Single-bar chart in FSI navy #1F3A5F, with the 38-state and two-territory coverage called out in the subtitle.

messages.content:
## 3. State Data: Texas

Texas is the only state that asks. The Texas Department of Public Safety records the immigration status of convicted offenders, which makes Texas the one jurisdiction in the country where conviction data can be set against the illegal immigrant population and read.

What the files show first is a measurement problem. Researchers at the Center for Immigration Studies who obtained DPS's prison-side records report that the state's published counts miss illegal immigrants who are identified only after they reach prison, and who are therefore tallied in a category the published conviction counts omit. Once those cases are added back, CIS finds the illegal immigrant homicide conviction rate in Texas runs above the statewide rate; in the 2015 data CIS analyzed, 20% higher.

Texas is also the exception. In the other 49 states the data do not exist, and the federal government does not collect them. Congress is being asked to fund an enforcement system whose own statistics cannot say how many convicted killers are in custody, in a country where only one state can say how many were convicted. What cannot be measured voluntarily can be mandated: DHS can be required to publish it.

## 4. Sanctuary Policies and Detainers

ICE cannot detain a criminal alien it never receives. The instrument is the detainer, a request that a jail hold a removable inmate for up to 48 hours past the local release date so ICE can take him into custody. In 2025, ICE issued 201,340 detainers to state and local law enforcement. In 17,864 cases the jurisdiction declined.

A declined detainer is a release decision. The person is already in criminal custody, already charged or convicted, and a local government hands him back to the neighborhood rather than to the agency that will remove him. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies count more than 25,000 declined detainers between Oct. 1, 2022, and Feb. 6, 2025. More than half of them, 52%, came from jails and prisons in California.

Cooperation is available and it works. ICE has signed 2,679 287(g) agreements with state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies covering 38 states and two U.S. territories as of October 2026. Where a jail honors a detainer, a removable criminal is transferred instead of released. Where it does not, the docket in Section 1 grows. Congress does not have to guess which jurisdictions fall into which category; ICE already keeps the tally, and it declines to publish it. The choice a sanctuary jurisdiction makes is not abstention. It is a decision, made on the public's behalf, that a removable criminal goes back to the street rather than into a van bound for a detention bed.

3. **Expand 287(g) to every willing agency.** Fund ICE's training pipeline so that every law enforcement agency that wants a jail enforcement, task force or warrant service officer agreement can sign one, and report to Congress annually on agencies still waiting for a signed agreement.
4. **Require DHS to publish the numbers.** Direct quarterly public reporting of the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, the current custody status of every noncitizen on it with a homicide conviction, and every declined detainer, by jurisdiction.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**

By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy

Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive Summary

- Federal data show 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities: noncitizens with homicide convictions who are not in ICE custody, on an agency docket that also carries 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025. Congress should fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, condition federal law enforcement money on detainer compliance, expand 287(g) and require DHS to publish the numbers it now withholds.

## 1. The Non-Detained Docket

Laken Riley went for a run on a campus trail in Athens, Georgia, on Feb. 22, 2024, and did not come home. Jose Ibarra, the illegal alien convicted that November of killing the 22-year-old nursing student, had entered the country unlawfully two years earlier. He is serving life in prison without parole. The policy question is not Ibarra's case. It is how many others like him were never taken into custody at all.

Federal data show 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities. That is ICE's own count of the noncitizens with homicide convictions on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, the most recent accounting ICE has provided to Congress. "Non-detained" means ICE has the file and is not holding the person. On the same date that docket listed 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions and another 1,845 charged with murder.

The figure is more than two years old because ICE has not updated it. The agency has never told Congress how many of the 13,099 are in a state or federal cell, how many were released under a sanctuary policy, or how long a homicide conviction keeps a noncitizen on the docket. Congress is holding a head count that ICE refuses to turn into a custody count.

Every name on that list is a person a judge or jury has already convicted, and whom the immigration system has already identified as removable. None of them is an unknown. Detention capacity is a spending decision, and the non-detained docket is the running total of what that decision costs. When an agency will not say where 13,099 convicted killers are, the deficit is not information. It is will. Every one of those files began with a victim, a police report and a prosecutor, and each of them represents a public safety judgment the federal government has already had the chance to make and did not make.

## 2. Federal Sentencing

The federal courts put a number on the same problem. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens. The U.S. Sentencing Commission counted 21,304 noncitizens among the individuals sentenced that year. Of those, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens.

Those sentences are convictions already obtained. Every one of the 21,304 is a person a federal court found guilty, and nearly nine in 10 of them had no lawful status in the country at all. A noncitizen share of the federal docket that large is not a rounding error. It is a distinct class of federal offender that Congress can see, count and address.

The count tracks federal prosecution, not the underlying population. GAO reported in October 2024 that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023 as federal criminal caseloads contracted. Even after that fall, 21,304 noncitizens were sentenced in a single fiscal year, in the federal system alone, on top of every state conviction. The federal number is the floor of the measurement, not the ceiling of the problem.

## 3. State Data: Texas

Texas is the only state that asks. The Texas Department of Public Safety records the immigration status of convicted offenders, which makes Texas the one jurisdiction in the country where conviction data can be set against the illegal immigrant population and read.

What the files show first is a measurement problem. Researchers at the Center for Immigration Studies who obtained DPS's prison-side records report that the state's published counts miss illegal immigrants who are identified only after they reach prison, and who are therefore tallied in a category the published conviction counts omit. Once those cases are added back, CIS finds the illegal immigrant homicide conviction rate in Texas runs above the statewide rate; in the 2015 data CIS analyzed, 20% higher.

Texas is also the exception. In the other 49 states the data do not exist, and the federal government does not collect them. Congress is being asked to fund an enforcement system whose own statistics cannot say how many convicted killers are in custody, in a country where only one state can say how many were convicted. What cannot be measured voluntarily can be mandated: DHS can be required to publish it.

## 4. Sanctuary Policies and Detainers

ICE cannot detain a criminal alien it never receives. The instrument is the detainer, a request that a jail hold a removable inmate for up to 48 hours past the local release date so ICE can take him into custody. In 2025, ICE issued 201,340 detainers to state and local law enforcement. In 17,864 cases the jurisdiction declined.

A declined detainer is a release decision. The person is already in criminal custody, already charged or convicted, and a local government hands him back to the neighborhood rather than to the agency that will remove him. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies count more than 25,000 declined detainers between Oct. 1, 2022, and Feb. 6, 2025. More than half of them, 52%, came from jails and prisons in California.

Cooperation is available and it works. ICE has signed 2,679 287(g) agreements with state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies covering 38 states and two U.S. territories as of October 2026. Where a jail honors a detainer, a removable criminal is transferred instead of released. Where it does not, the docket in Section 1 grows. Congress does not have to guess which jurisdictions fall into which category; ICE already keeps the tally, and it declines to publish it. The choice a sanctuary jurisdiction makes is not abstention. It is a decision, made on the public's behalf, that a removable criminal goes back to the street rather than into a van bound for a detention bed.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention capacity earmarked for noncitizens on the non-detained docket who have criminal convictions, and direct ICE to take them into custody as beds come online, homicide convictions first.
2. **Condition federal law enforcement funding on detainer compliance.** Require state and local recipients of federal justice funding to honor ICE detainers and to notify ICE before releasing a removable inmate; withhold funds from jurisdictions that refuse, and restore eligibility when the policy changes.
3. **Expand 287(g) to every willing agency.** Fund ICE's training pipeline so that every law enforcement agency that wants a jail enforcement, task force or warrant service officer agreement can sign one, and report to Congress annually on agencies still waiting for a signed agreement.
4. **Require DHS to publish the numbers.** Direct quarterly public reporting of the size and criminal composition of the non-detained docket, the current custody status of every noncitizen on it with a homicide conviction, and every declined detainer, by jurisdiction.

*Data for every figure in this brief appear in the accompanying data appendix.*

**WASHINGTON (Oct. 27, 2026)** - Federal data show 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities, and Congress has the tools to put that number down, according to a new brief from the Founders' Square Institute.

"Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, is by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy. It draws on ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, GAO and Texas DPS data.

ICE's non-detained docket listed 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions and 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions as of July 21, 2024, the most recent accounting ICE has given Congress, and the agency has not said how many are behind bars.

More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025 out of 201,340 issued.

"These are not allegations, and they are not estimates," Kessler said. "They are convictions the government has already obtained, and people it has already identified as removable. ICE keeps a head count and refuses to turn it into a custody count. Congress should fund the custody, condition federal money on detainer compliance and make DHS publish what it now withholds."

The brief recommends that Congress fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, condition federal law enforcement funding on detainer compliance, expand 287(g) to every willing agency, and require quarterly public reporting on the docket and every declined detainer.

The brief, its data appendix and a fact sheet for Hill offices will be posted at [FSI LINK] when the embargo lifts.

The Founders' Square Institute is a Washington, D.C. public-policy think tank.
